hints: Notice the exact wording gravitational force on the astronaut, not the force felt from the seat or floor during the $0.2g$ launch.
Recall $F = mg$ depends on astronaut mass $m$ and gravitational field strength $g$ near the launchpad, not on the spacecraft acceleration.
Compare the unchanged pull of the Earth with the larger upward push needed from the seat to produce net upward acceleration of $0.2g$.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: the gravitational force $F = mg$ due to the Earth, not the apparent weight felt in the accelerating spacecraft.
State the rule: gravitational force depends on mass $m$ and local gravitational field strength $g$. The spacecraft acceleration of $0.2g$ upwards does not change $m$ or $g$ just after launch.
Therefore just after launch $F$ is still approximately $mg$, with the same units of newtons.
Note the distractor: the seat must push up harder to accelerate the astronaut, giving contact force $R - mg = m(0.2g)$ so $R = 1.2mg$. That is apparent weight, not gravitational force.
So the gravitational force remains $mg$. This is option B.

options.A: This $1.2mg$ is the contact force from the seat, not the gravitational force. It gives the extra $0.2mg$ needed for upward acceleration.
options.B: Gravitational force is $F = mg$ and depends only on mass and $g$. Just after launch $g$ is almost unchanged, so it stays $mg$.
options.C: Subtracting $0.2mg$ from $mg$ has no physical basis here. The acceleration adds to the required contact force, it does not reduce gravity.
options.D: Zero would mean no gravity or complete weightlessness in orbit. At launch near the Earth the gravitational field still acts.
